title: Goldman Sachs Expects `Strong Rebound' for Stocks
description: Apr.08 -- Goldman Sachs says equities have further to fall before a "strong rebound" driven by a 50% plus rise in corporate earnings in the U.S. and Europe, as well as an increase in dividend payouts. "It's that improvement into the future that the market is not yet really reflecting, particularly on the dividend story," Peter Oppenheimer, the bank's chief global equity strategist, said on "Bloomberg Markets: European Open."

asr.full_text: I was listening to Ben Bernanke a former a former chair, of course saying it's not like the depression this isn't going to last for 12 years but he did say if all goes well in a year or two we should be in a substantially better position do we have to start thinking about things over that kind of time horizon? Well I think it's I think that's right we do believe that we will get out of this and the recovery will be quite strong, but the dip in the meantime is pretty significant. I mean, to give a scale of it, we're looking at US GDP falling by 6.2% this year, 9% across the Eurozone, and globally a contraction of 1.8%, and that's in GDP terms. And we're expecting earnings to fall by about a third in the US and by 45% because the eurozone over 20% because Asia these are very big numbers relative to even other recessions the financial crisis and one of those parts because this is effectively a stopping of demand, from which there should be a recovery, so long as there isn't too much second-round effect damage in the economy during the period of lockdowns, we would expect quite a strong rebound after. So, earnings picking up next year by 50%-plus in the US and Europe, and alongside that, some improvement in dividends. And it's that improvement into the future that the market is not yet really reflecting, particularly on the dividend story. But we do expect to see global growth next year rising by over 6 percent. It won't take us back to the starting levels, but I do think that that's a prospect which will trigger, we think, quite a strong rebound in equities, but from a lower level than they are currently. Peter, how can that be when you have companies and consumers around the world that are now that are getting no income, no revenues, and getting loaded up with debt that has strings attached? I mean, it, on the other side of this crisis, they're going to come out with more debt than probably they've ever had before. How does that drive in the economy? Well, I think, again, we need to be careful making a distinction between growth rate and levels of growth. So from a very, very low base, effectively you have large parts of Maine economies in Moscow doing nothing at all. As you get some relaxation of mobility, demand should pick up and you should get quite a strong growth rate. But you won't get back to the previous trend rates of growth for a very long time and that would be true for profits as well. So even though, for example, we expect earnings per share having fallen 45% across Europe this year, to give an example and a 50% rise next year. Even by the end of the year after that, the actual level of earnings per share would still be below the peak that it reached back in 2007. So I think there's a difference between the growth rate from a very low base and then the pace of growth thereafter. But to your point on taking on debt, which is true for many companies and, of course, the governments themselves, I think this does serve as well to demonstrate the importance or the value attributed to companies with strong balance sheets that at least will be in the position to be able to generate stable cash flows and pay dividends into the future. These companies are benefiting on a relative basis. That's true in the credit market, as well as the equity market. While that's understandable in a time of greater uncertainty in a recession, we still think that would be true coming out of this, for the reasons that you suggest.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents Bloomberg financial-news analysis in which Goldman Sachs strategist Peter Oppenheimer discusses market declines, economic contraction, and a conditional possibility of stronger future growth. The segment includes qualified stock and earnings forecasts, including a significant dip and non-sharp recovery, without a promised return, required payment, requested credentials, or directed participation mechanism.
